philosophy.summary: BitTorrent infohashes are deterministic given controlled inputs (file content, piece length, torrent name, file order). This mirrors IPFS CID determinism — same content always produces same hash.
philosophy.quote: That's it. Nothing inherently non-deterministic in there. So if you control: file content (guaranteed identical by IPFS), piece length (deterministic formula), torrent name (use CID), file ordering (alphabetical), no non-deterministic fields in info dict — then you get the same infohash every time.

philosophy.topic: Separation of concerns in distributed systems
philosophy.summary: Compute services (torrent generation) should be distinct from business logic services (wiki bot). Each owns its domain: delivery-kid owns IPFS + hashing, Blue Railroad owns wiki page editing. This keeps audit trails clean and responsibilities clear.
philosophy.quote: Delivery-kid shouldn't be editing wiki pages at all — that's Blue Railroad's job. So the architecture should be: Delivery-kid: 'Give me a CID, I'll generate a torrent and return the infohash' — pure compute service. Blue Railroad: Queries PickiPedia for releases missing torrents, calls delivery-kid for each CID, updates the wiki pages under its own bot account

philosophy.summary: YAML manipulation is risky; comprehensive tests (152 passing) verify string-append strategy preserves formatting, idempotency, and valid YAML output. Tests prevent surprise wiki reformats.
philosophy.quote: The critical thing the tests verify: `append_torrent_fields` reads the YAML to check state but **writes by string append**, so existing formatting is never touched.

philosophy.summary: Expensive compute endpoints (IPFS fetch + SHA-1 hashing) should require authentication to prevent DoS. Public data (CID, deterministic hash) is not the concern — server resources are.
philosophy.quote: An unauthenticated endpoint that triggers that kind of work is a DoS vector. Someone could spam it with CIDs and tie up the pinning service. The data itself is public (IPFS content, deterministic hash), so there's no secret being protected. It's the server resources you're protecting.

philosophy.summary: BT clients can bootstrap from IPFS gateways (BEP 19 webseeds) without requiring a dedicated BitTorrent seeder. Dual webseeds (fast local + fallback public) provide good UX without infrastructure overhead.
philosophy.quote: This isn't the same as a proper BitTorrent seed — there's no peer announcing to trackers, no swarm participation. But it means anyone with the magnet link can actually download the files immediately, which is the important thing.

portrait: This tail traces magent's work on BitTorrent integration for PickiPedia, moving through multiple architectural iterations driven by justin's corrections. Magent initially proposed a finalize-pipeline approach, then a cron reconciliation, but justin steered toward a lightweight HTTP endpoint on delivery-kid. A major discovery came when magent found maybelle/pinning-service (dead code) and learned the real Blue Railroad logic lives in a separate repository. This prompted a critical refactoring: delivery-kid became a pure compute service (torrent generation), while Blue Railroad retained wiki editing responsibilities under its bot account. Magent built thorough tests (152 passing) to prevent unwanted YAML reformatting and proposed a surgical string-append strategy instead of round-tripping. The session ended with discussion of IPFS block storage format and BitTorrent webseeds as a graceful-degradation strategy for bootstrap without dedicated seeders.
